title: Cortical Loss Functions

html:
Before examining how the cortex computes and propagates error signals, we must specify what it is optimizing–the objective functions or "loss functions" whose minimization defines what "good" networks accomplish. Talking about a loss function for cortex is necessarily a normative move: cortical tissue does not (and need not) compute a single scalar objective and backpropagate its gradient. Instead, the cortex implements a family of locally computable discrepancy measures whose combined effect can be interpreted as optimizing an implicit objective. Several overlapping normative proposals have accumulated over the past half-century–redundancy reduction, efficient coding, sparse coding, slow feature analysis, infomax, prediction error minimization–that might at first appear to be competing theories. A central theoretical achievement of the last two decades has been to show that most of these can be understood as components of, or special cases of, a single unifying objective: the minimization of variational free energy in a hierarchical generative model 1, 2, 3. A complementary unifying move is that cortical prediction is inherently sensorimotor: perception is an action-based hypothesis-testing process, so predictions (and hence local losses) are conditioned not only on latent causes but also on impending and executed actions (via efference copy and feedback). This motivates active predictive coding (APC) as a cortical loss framing in which both sensory and action prediction errors can drive inference and learning 4. The remainder of this section unpacks models of core cortical loss functions, identifies the additional implicit costs (metabolic, homeostatic) that shape the biological loss landscape, and examines how the effective loss varies across cortical areas, timescales, and neuromodulatory states. A 2026 computational model tests local error-neuron microcircuits (Figure) 83. The model tests a predictive-coding implementation (Figure).

The most comprehensive normative account of cortical learning casts it as approximate Bayesian inference in a hierarchical generative model of the sensorium 1, 2, 5, 6. The cortex is hypothesized to maintain an internal generative model pθ(x,z1,...,zL)p_\theta(x,z_1,...,z_L) that specifies how latent causes zlz_l at multiple hierarchical levels conspire to generate sensory observations xx. Because exact Bayesian posterior inference–computing p(z∣x)p(z∣x)–is intractable for any model of realistic complexity, the cortex instead maintains an approximate posterior qϕ(z|x)q_\phi(z|x), parameterized by neural activity patterns (for fast online inference) and synaptic weights (for slow model learning), and minimizes the variational free energy:

F=DKL[qϕ(z∣x)∥pθ(z)]⏟complexity−𝔼qϕ[log⁡pθ(x∣z)]⏟accuracy\begin{equation} F \;=\; \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl[q_\phi(z \mid x)\;\|\;p_\theta(z)\bigr]}_{\text{complexity}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\!\bigl[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\bigr]}_{\text{accuracy}} \end{equation}

The first term (complexity) is the information/description-length cost of encoding xx into latents zz–how far the posterior q(z∣x)q(z∣x) must move away from the prior p(z)p(z) (i.e., how many extra nats/bits the representation uses beyond what the model expects a priori). The second term (accuracy) is the model’s expected fit to the data under the inferred latents–how well samples z∼q(z|x)z\sim q(z|x) can predict/reconstruct xx (equivalently, its negative is the expected reconstruction error / negative log-likelihood). Since F≥−log⁡pθ(x)F\ge-\log{p_\theta(x)} (variational free energy upper-bounds surprisal, equivalently negative log-model-evidence) minimizing FF simultaneously tightens the variational bound (making qϕq_\phi a better approximation to the true posterior) and increases model evidence (making pθp_\theta a better model of the data). In this framework, cortical inference and cortical learning are two faces of the same optimization–free energy minimization–operating on different timescales: fast neural dynamics update activity patterns to minimize FF for fixed weights (inference/perception, on the order of hundreds of milliseconds), while slower synaptic plasticity updates weights to minimize FF averaged across data (learning, on the order of minutes to years) 1, 2, 6.

Decomposition into precision-weighted prediction errors

Under the Laplace approximation (Gaussian posteriors parameterized by their means, with estimated covariance structure) and a hierarchical generative model in which each level predicts the level below via xl̂=fθ(zt+1)\hat{x_l}=f_\theta(z_{t+1}), the variational free energy decomposes into a sum of local, precision-weighted prediction-error terms 7, 1, 8:

F≈∑l=0L[12𝜺l⊤𝚷l𝜺l+12ln|𝚷l−1|]\begin{equation} F \;\approx\; \sum_{l=0}^{L} \left[\frac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l^\top\,\boldsymbol{\Pi}_l\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l \;+\; \frac{1}{2}\ln\!\bigl|\boldsymbol{\Pi}_l^{-1}\bigr|\right] \end{equation}

where 𝜺l=𝒙𝒍−𝒙𝒍̂\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l=\boldsymbol{x_l}-\boldsymbol{\hat{x_l}} is the prediction error at level ll (the mismatch between the representation at that level and the top-down prediction generated by level l+1l+1), and 𝚷l\boldsymbol{\Pi}_l is the precision matrix (inverse covariance) encoding the expected reliability of predictions at that level. The first term within each summand is the precision-weighted squared prediction error: large, high-precision mismatches incur a heavy cost and drive strong updates, while equally large but low-precision mismatches (attributed to noise) incur little cost. The second term–the log-determinant of the covariance–penalizes overconfident precision estimates, preventing the degenerate solution of simply setting all precisions to zero (which would trivially zero-out the first term by declaring all predictions unreliable, but would incur unbounded cost under the second term). Though this log-determinant term is frequently omitted in simplified treatments, it is normatively essential for a self-consistent system that must learn both the content of its predictions and their reliability 1, 9 (precision is covered in depth in the next section ("Cortical Error Signals")). The critical computational insight is that the global free energy decomposes into a sum of local losses, each defined at a single hierarchical level using only locally available quantities: the top-down prediction from the level above and the bottom-up representation at the current level. This level-wise decomposition is the feature that makes hierarchical predictive coding biologically plausible as a cortical learning principle. No single neuron or cortical area needs to compute, store, or have access to the global loss; each area simply needs to compare its current representation with predictions arriving via feedback connections from hierarchically adjacent areas, compute a local mismatch, and adjust synaptic weights to reduce that mismatch. The aggregate effect of these local updates, carried out across all levels simultaneously, is to reduce the global free energy.

The precision matrices 𝚷l\boldsymbol{\Pi}_l appearing in Eq. 2 are not fixed hyperparameters but estimated quantities encoding the expected reliability (inverse variance) of predictions at each hierarchical level; functionally, they act as a gain field over error units, amplifying "trustworthy" mismatches and down-weighting those attributable to noise or irrelevant degrees of freedom 10, 1, 8. The cortex therefore does not simply "reduce prediction error" but "reduce precision-weighted prediction error," so the effective loss landscape is continually reshaped by inferred uncertainty. Several partially redundant biological mechanisms–neuromodulatory gain control, apical dendritic gating, oscillatory synchrony, population-level variability suppression, and thalamocortical precision gating via the pulvinar–implement this precision weighting on overlapping timescales ranging from tens of milliseconds to minutes (details deferred to the "Cortical Error Signals" section). Their joint action ensures that the cortical loss function is inherently adaptive and context-dependent: the same magnitude of prediction error 𝜺l\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_l can drive vigorous synaptic updating in one behavioral state and be effectively ignored in another, depending on the precision assigned by these converging mechanisms. This precision-weighting framework has also been proposed as the computational basis of attention: attending to a stimulus or modality corresponds to increasing 𝚷l\boldsymbol{\Pi}_l for the corresponding prediction-error units, thereby amplifying their influence on both fast inference and slow synaptic learning–recasting spatial, feature-based, and expectation-driven attentional modulation as different patterns of precision deployment across the cortical hierarchy 10, 11, 12.

Temporal framing

A static, instantaneous prediction-error loss is insufficient for cortical learning. The world is not a succession of independent snapshots; environmental causes evolve continuously according to dynamical laws that span a vast range of timescales–from the millisecond acoustics of a phoneme to the minutes-long arc of a social narrative to the seasonal rhythms that shape foraging and migration. Kiebel, Daunizeau, and Friston proposed that cortical anatomy recapitulates the temporal hierarchy inherent in the dynamics of environmental states: the lowest levels correspond to fast fluctuations associated with sensory processing, whereas the highest levels encode slow contextual changes under which faster representations unfold 13. A cortex that merely minimized the mismatch between its current prediction and the current sensory state–with no representation of how those states change–would be perpetually surprised by any structured temporal sequence, unable to distinguish an expected continuation from a genuine novelty. The loss function must therefore be extended along the temporal axis in at least three complementary ways: (i) the generative model must encode dynamics–not only "what" but "what next" and "how fast"; (ii) the hierarchical decomposition of the loss must assign different levels to different temporal scales; and (iii) the system must, in some regimes, look forward in time, evaluating anticipated future prediction errors to guide action selection and policy optimization. A 2025 cortical model tests temporal self-supervised prediction and identifies the pathways required for learning (Figure) 82. A 2025 cortical model tests temporal self-supervised prediction and identifies the pathways required for learning (Figure). A dynamic predictive-coding model represents sequences hierarchically (Figure) 84. The model learns from natural video sequences (Figure).

The first extension amounts to replacing a static generative model with a hierarchical dynamical model–one whose hidden states have equations of motion and whose predictions therefore concern not just the current value of sensory input but its trajectory. Formally, this replaces a static likelihood pθ(x∣z)p_\theta(x\mid z) with a state-space (or controlled state-space) model:

zt+1=fθ(zt,at)+ωt,xt=gθ(zt)+νt,\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} z_{t+1} &= f_\theta(z_t, a_t) + \omega_t, \\ x_t &= g_\theta(z_t) + \nu_t, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where ata_t denotes action, and ωt,νt\omega_t,\nu_t are process and observation noise 14. Importantly, the inclusion of ata_t in the state-transition function is not merely a convenience for modeling overtly motor tasks; recent evidence suggests it is a canonical feature of cortical computation. Rao proposed active predictive coding (APC), which posits that every cortical area maintains both a state-transition network f̂s\hat{f}_s (predicting the next latent state given the current state and action) and an action-prediction (policy) network f̂a\hat{f}_a (mapping state estimates to actions or abstract goals) 4. This is motivated by converging empirical findings showing that action signals are ubiquitous across cortical areas: widefield calcium imaging reveals bilateral activation across cortical areas—including primary visual cortex—preceding movement on choice trials 15; spiking activity in nearly all recorded cortical regions contains neurons whose firing is predictive of upcoming movements 16; and approximately one-third of population activity variance in mouse visual cortex can be predicted from ongoing motor behavior 17. Even at the laminar level, both L2/3 and L5/6 neurons in mouse V1 depolarize before locomotion onset, with layer-specific differences consistent with visuomotor comparison (L2/3) versus integration (L5/6) 18. These observations support the APC claim that the action term ata_t in the cortical generative model is not restricted to traditional motor areas but is present at every level of the cortical hierarchy, making the state-transition function fs(st−1,at−1)f_s(s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) a canonical cortical computation rather than an optional extension for motor control.

Friston and Kiebel generalized hierarchical predictive coding to cover dynamics in the world by formulating generative models in generalized coordinates of motion, which lends them a hierarchical form in both structure and dynamics 11. In generalized coordinates, the brain represents not just the immediate observation state but all time derivatives: position, velocity, acceleration, jerk, and so on 19. Equivalently, observations and hidden states are represented as generalized vectors:

x̃t:=(xt,ẋt,ẍt,…),z̃t:=(zt,żt,z̈t,…).\begin{equation} \tilde{x}_t := (x_t,\dot{x}_t,\ddot{x}_t,\ldots), \qquad \tilde{z}_t := (z_t,\dot{z}_t,\ddot{z}_t,\ldots). \end{equation} Under a Laplace (Gaussian) approximation to the posterior, the resulting free energy decomposes into prediction errors over these generalized orders of motion, each weighted by a corresponding precision that encodes the expected smoothness of the dynamics at that order 11, 10, 9. Under this approximation, free energy can be expressed as a sum over hierarchical levels ll and derivative orders kk: F≈∑l∑k≥0[12εl(k)⊤Πl(k)εl(k)+12ln|Πl(k)−1|],\begin{equation} F \;\approx\; \sum_{l}\sum_{k\ge 0}\left[\frac{1}{2}\,{\varepsilon}_{l}^{(k)\top}\,\Pi_{l}^{(k)}\,{\varepsilon}_{l}^{(k)} \;+\; \frac{1}{2}\ln\!\bigl|\Pi_{l}^{(k)-1}\bigr|\right], \end{equation} where εl(k){\varepsilon}_{l}^{(k)} denotes the prediction error for the kk-th temporal derivative at level ll. The update equations become a form of generalized Bayesian filtering: neural dynamics track a moving target through generalized coordinates, and under linear-Gaussian assumptions predictive-coding updates recover Kalman-Bucy-style filtering dynamics (i.e precision-weighted prediction-error correction as a filter) 11. The practical consequence is that temporal prediction errors–mismatches between expected and observed rates of change–become additional terms in the cortical loss, and they recruit the same hierarchical error-correction machinery (superficial pyramidal error units, deep-layer prediction units) that was described for instantaneous prediction. Simulations of this scheme show, for instance, a vigorous expression of prediction error after an expected sensory event is omitted, reflecting the dynamical nature of the recognition process: the model continues to predict what should have come next, even in the absence of input 11. This omission-response phenomenology has been supported empirically: human auditory cortex and frontal regions exhibit a hierarchical organization of prediction and novelty-detection systems, with early mismatch negativity (MMN) reflecting local auditory predictions and later P3b responses reflecting more global, temporally integrative violations of expectation 20. Intracranial recordings have directly demonstrated this hierarchy: temporal cortex responds to any change in immediate stimulus history, whereas frontal cortex responds exclusively to globally unpredictable changes spanning longer timescales 21.

The second extension–the assignment of different hierarchical levels to different temporal scales–connects the formal structure of the loss to the large-scale anatomy of the cortex. The environment is composed of coupled dynamical processes whose characteristic rates span orders of magnitude. In the framework of Kiebel et al., the generative model is itself hierarchical in time: fast sensory fluctuations are generated by low-level attractors whose dynamics are modulated by the states of slower, higher-level attractors, which in turn are controlled by still slower contextual variables 13. The model develops representations on different timescales (Figure). A three-level version learns progressively abstract temporal features (Figure).

Empirical evidence for temporal receptive windows (TRWs). Hasson and colleagues introduced the concept of the temporal receptive window–the duration over which accumulated sensory information influences a cortical area’s response–and showed that it increases systematically from sensory to association cortex 22. Early visual cortex exhibited high response reliability regardless of disruptions in temporal structure, whereas higher areas were sensitive to temporal scrambling 22. Lerner et al. extended this to auditory-language cortex using temporally scrambled narratives: early auditory cortex (A1) was driven by momentary input regardless of scrambling condition, intermediate areas required sentence-level coherence, and apex areas (parietal and frontal cortex) responded reliably only when intact paragraphs were heard in meaningful sequence–suggesting that the timescale of processing is a general organizing principle of the human cerebral cortex 23. Importantly, superposition of visual and auditory TRW maps revealed that this orderly hierarchy is a general topographic organization principle of the human cortex, spanning modalities 23. During spoken narrative comprehension, a fixed temporal sequence of response lags–on the scale of several seconds–propagates from early auditory cortex to language areas, the attention network, and finally the default mode network, directly demonstrating hierarchical information flow along the cortical timescale gradient 24.

Intrinsic neural timescales (INTs). A crucial advance beyond stimulus-driven TRWs was the discovery by Murray et al. that the timescale hierarchy is not merely imposed by task structure but is an intrinsic property of cortical dynamics. They measured timescales of intrinsic fluctuations in spiking activity across macaque cortical areas and found a hierarchical ordering, with sensory and prefrontal areas exhibiting shorter and longer timescales, respectively–suggesting that intrinsic timescales reflect areal specialization for computations over multiple temporal ranges 25. These intrinsic timescales set the duration over which a neural circuit integrates its inputs: shorter timescales in sensory areas enable rapid tracking of dynamic stimuli, whereas prefrontal areas can integrate information over longer timescales to improve signal-to-noise in working memory and decision-making 25. Temporal specialization arises from a region’s intrinsic dynamics–dynamics present even in the absence of direct sensory stimulation–revealing a hierarchical progression from fast timescales in sensory areas to slower timescales in association areas 26. Moreover, neuronal timescales are not static: transmembrane current timescales across association regions increase during working memory delay periods, and working memory performance is predicted by the extent of timescale increase in prefrontal cortex 27. Multiple timescales may arise from recurrent spatial connectivity within a cortical area and flexibly change with cognitive state: attention can lengthen the slow intrinsic timescale in V4, and these changes correlate with behavioral performance 28. A 2025 preprint measures neural timescales across the mouse brain (Figure) 85. The preprint maps timescales across brain regions (Figure).

But what determines the intrinsic timescale of a cortical area? A convergent picture has emerged from anatomy, transcriptomics, and computational modeling, pointing to at least four interacting mechanisms: The preprint relates timescales to task-variable encoding (Figure). The preprint compares timescales with anatomical structure (Figure).

Gradient of recurrent excitatory synaptic strength. Chaudhuri et al. developed a large-scale dynamical model of macaque neocortex in which both local and inter-regional circuit mechanisms contributed to a hierarchy of timescales; a particularly important feature was that regions higher in the cortical hierarchy were endowed with stronger local excitatory connection strength, motivated by the empirical observation that pyramidal neurons in these regions possess a greater number of dendritic spines 29, 30, 31. A hierarchy of timescales naturally emerged from this system: sensory areas showed brief, transient responses (appropriate for sensory processing), whereas association areas integrated inputs over time and exhibited persistent activity (suitable for decision-making and working memory) 30. Mechanistically, stronger recurrent connections slow intrinsic dynamics by partially canceling leak currents, and there are confirmed increases across the cortical hierarchy in the number and density of excitatory synapses onto pyramidal cells, likely reflecting increased recurrent strength across areas 25, 31. Human intracranial recordings reveal a timescale gradient (Figure). The study relates timescales to cortical gene-expression gradients (Figure).

NMDA receptor composition and synaptic kinetics. NMDA receptors in the recurrent circuits of prefrontal cortex exhibit roughly twofold longer decay time-constants than those in primary visual cortex and temporally summate trains of stimuli more effectively 32. More generally, intrinsic timescale appears to depend not just on the amount of NMDA-mediated recurrence, but on its subunit composition: higher-order cortex shows hierarchy-linked enrichment of GRIN2B/GluN2B-related excitation 33, 34, and GluN2B-containing NMDARs deactivate much more slowly than GluN2A-containing receptors while coupling especially strongly to CaMKII-dependent plasticity signaling 35, 36. This helps explain why persistent activity in association cortex is thought to arise from attractor states sustained by NMDA-mediated recurrent excitation coupled with fast feedback inhibition 27, 37. The implication for learning is direct: areas with slower, more GluN2B-weighted NMDA kinetics implement a broader temporal integration kernel, so their prediction-error signals and eligibility traces can accumulate discrepancies over longer windows before being converted into synaptic change.

Inter-areal connectivity and network architecture. The Chaudhuri et al. model was built on quantitative directed and weighted connectivity data, and the hierarchy of timescales emerged from the combination of local heterogeneity and specific inter-areal projection profiles; moreover, slower prefrontal and temporal areas had a disproportionate impact on global brain dynamics 30. Importantly, the synaptic dynamics of backward connections have slower time constants; forward connections are driving and elicit obligatory responses, whereas backward connections have both driving and modulatory effects and operate over larger spatial and temporal scales 11. This asymmetry is exactly what the temporal free-energy framework requires: feedback predictions encode slowly changing contextual priors that constrain faster inference at the levels below.

Cell-intrinsic and neuromodulatory properties. A longer intrinsic timescale can also reflect timescales of cellular or synaptic dynamics; consistent with this, there are interareal differences in the dynamical properties of recurrent excitatory synapses, including differential composition of glutamate receptors, expression of short-term synaptic plasticity, and level of neuromodulation, as well as interareal differences in cellular physiology driven by factors such as neuronal morphology 25. Areal specialization for timescales of learning is potentially shaped by gradients in the densities of receptors for neuromodulators including dopamine and serotonin 38, 39. Spike-frequency adaptation, voltage-gated ion channels with diverse time constants, and the balance of tonic versus phasic inhibition all contribute additional degrees of freedom. A primate study tests whether attention changes neural timescales (Figure). The study relates timescales to reaction time (Figure).

In sum, the cortical hierarchy of intrinsic timescales is not a single-mechanism phenomenon but an emergent property of graded anatomy (spine density, NMDA composition, myelination), large-scale directed connectivity, and cell-intrinsic biophysics—all of which are themselves organized along the macroscopic principal gradient from sensory to transmodal cortex.

The third temporal extension of the loss function concerns the future. Standard variational free energy scores the fit between the generative model and past and present observations (i.e between priors and present beliefs); it is backward-looking by construction. But organisms must also evaluate policies–sequences of prospective actions–in terms of their anticipated consequences. Active inference addresses this by positing that the brain uses its generative model to predict incoming sensory data, and the fit between model and data may be improved either by optimizing beliefs (perceptual inference) or by acting on the world to change the data; this implies a common objective (minimizing variational free energy) for both action and perception 40. Policy selection becomes a form of Bayesian model selection, where the evidence for a particular policy is the free energy expected in the future–an unusual objective because it scores policies based on outcomes that have yet to be observed 40. This is typically expressed by defining the expected free energy (EFE) of a policy π\pi at future time τ\tau: A 2026 active-inference model simulates hypothesis selection (Figure) 86. The model tests the role of expected information gain (Figure).

Gτ(π):=𝔼q(oτ,sτ∣π)[lnq(sτ∣π)−lnp(oτ,sτ)],\begin{equation} G_\tau(\pi) \;:=\; \mathbb{E}_{q(o_\tau,s_\tau\mid \pi)}\!\left[\ln q(s_\tau\mid \pi)\;-\;\ln p(o_\tau,s_\tau)\right], \end{equation} with policy selection often written as q(π)∝exp⁡(−γ∑τGτ(π))q(\pi)\propto \exp(-\gamma\,\sum_\tau G_\tau(\pi)) for an inverse-temperature γ\gamma. The expected free energy is a central quantity in active inference: agents select policies that minimize G(π)G(\pi), and its decomposition captures the exploration-exploitation tradeoff 41. A common decomposition separates an epistemic value term (expected information gain about hidden states) from an extrinsic/pragmatic value term induced by prior preferences over outcomes p(oτ)p(o_\tau); outcomes are "valuable" insofar as they are assigned high prior probability by these preferences, and "costly" insofar as they are surprising under them 42. This forward-looking extension of the loss has direct implications for the cortical timescale hierarchy: agents decide between temporally deep policies, where temporal depth refers to the depth of the planning horizon 40. Prefrontal and default-mode regions–those at the apex of the temporal receptive window hierarchy–are the natural candidates for representing expected free energy over extended planning horizons, consistent with their role in prospective thinking, counterfactual reasoning, and goal-directed behavior (EFE discussed more in the "Superordinate Objectives" section).

It is worth emphasizing that the expected free energy is not a second, independent objective: it is the natural forward-looking extension of the same variational quantity defined in Eq. 1. Structurally, both VFE and EFE share the generic form 𝔼q[ln⁡q−ln⁡p]\mathbb{E}_q[\ln q-\ln p]; the crucial difference lies in what grounds the expectation. VFE is conditioned on actual observations xx already received: it scores how well current beliefs qϕ(z|x)q_\phi(z|x) explain real data, and is minimized by perceptual inference and synaptic learning. EFE, by contrast, is conditioned on a policy π\pi and taken over predicted future observations oτo_\tau and states sτs_\tau that the generative model expects to encounter if that policy is executed: it scores the anticipated quality of those encounters, and is minimized by policy selection. (Here, oτo_\tau and sτs_\tau correspond to the observations x and latent states z of the VFE formulation, now indexed by a future time τ and conditioned on an action sequence.) A second, substantive difference is that the joint model p(oτ,sτ)p(o_\tau,s_\tau) entering EFE incorporates prior preferences p(oτ)p(o_\tau)–an explicit specification of which sensory outcomes the agent treats as desirable–that have no direct analogue in the backward-looking VFE, which merely fits a generative model to whatever data arrive. It is these prior preferences that inject goal-directedness into policy selection: without them, EFE would reduce to pure epistemic foraging (maximizing information gain), with no drive toward biologically or task-relevant outcomes. Parr and Friston formalized the connection between VFE and EFE through the generalised free energy, which unifies the two within a single objective that transitions smoothly from assimilating present evidence (VFE-dominant) to evaluating potential futures (EFE-dominant) 40. Operationally, the two quantities interlock in a perception-action cycle: EFE-based policy selection determines the agent’s next action; that action generates new sensory data; VFE minimization then assimilates those data into updated beliefs; and the cycle repeats–making VFE and EFE two temporally complementary faces of a single imperative to minimize surprise across time.

A further temporal-framing move is chunking: rather than treating experience as a purely continuous stream, cortex appears to infer discrete latent "events" with relatively stable internal statistics, separated by boundaries where latent causes change. Data-driven neural-state segmentation during narrative perception reveals a nested event hierarchy: short events in sensory regions and longer events in high-order regions that encode abstract situation models 43. This suggests a complementary picture to generalized-coordinate tracking: cortical hierarchies may combine (i) continuous-time trajectory tracking within an event with (ii) discrete latent-state transitions at event boundaries, where large prediction errors can trigger model reconfiguration and accelerated updating.

In synthesis, the cortical loss function is not a single, static, instantaneous error signal. It is a temporally deep, hierarchically factorized objective that encompasses: (i) instantaneous prediction errors at each hierarchical level, weighted by level-specific precisions; (ii) dynamical prediction errors over generalized coordinates of motion, penalizing mismatches in the predicted trajectory, not just the current state; (iii) a hierarchy of temporal scales, anchored by the intrinsic timescale gradient of cortical areas, such that each level of the hierarchy is "assigned" to minimize prediction error over a characteristic temporal window; (iv) an anticipated or expected free energy that extends the loss into the future, guiding action and policy selection toward states that are both information-rich (epistemically valuable) and consistent with prior preferences (pragmatically valuable); and (v) event-level discretization that compresses long streams into latent-state segments. This is how a predictive cortex can remain locally error-driven while still being genuinely temporally deep.

From Hierarchical Levels to Heterarchical Graphs

The preceding paragraphs have formalized the cortical loss as a sum over hierarchical levels: each level sends predictions downward and receives prediction errors upward. This is a powerful abstraction, but it is not the only (or even the most faithful) way to formalize what cortex is doing. The anatomical reality is a dense, recurrent, skip-connected, multi-area graph with parallel cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamo-cortical pathways, abundant lateral connections within areas, and skip connections that routinely bypass intermediate levels (e.g via transthalamic cortico-pulvino-cortical routing 44). A useful generalization is therefore: cortex is a distributed inference-and-learning engine that performs variational message passing on a structured graphical model, where "hierarchies" are a special case–a convenient coordinate system imposed on a richer heterarchical substrate 45, 46. Nothing in the core computational idea of predictive coding–compare locally predicted activity against locally observed activity; pass mismatches; iterate until consistency–requires a chain-like hierarchy. One can write a generative model over any directed graph (including loopy graphs with lateral and skip connections), perform inference by iterative "relaxation" (coordinate descent on a variational objective), and update synapses with local Hebbian-like rules driven by pre/post activity and local errors. Recent work makes this explicit: predictive-coding-style inference and learning can be defined on arbitrary graph topologies, i.e., on the kind of heterarchical wiring patterns that real neocortex exhibits 47, and can approximate (and, in certain limits, converge to) backpropagation-style gradients using only local information 48 (framed elsewhere as "reverse-mode differentiation" on arbitrary computation graphs 49). Concretely, the global free energy generalizes from a sum over hierarchical levels to a sum over nodes in a directed graph:

F=∑i∈𝒱Fi,Fi=12𝜺i⊤𝚷i𝜺i+12ln⁡|𝚷i−1|,\begin{equation} F \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}} F_i, \qquad F_i \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i^\top\, \boldsymbol{\Pi}_i\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\!\bigl|\boldsymbol{\Pi}_i^{-1}\bigr|, \end{equation} where each node ii’s local loss FiF_i is determined entirely by signals available at its afferents, and the graph (𝒱,ℰ)(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) can include lateral, skip, and recurrent edges without altering the form of the local update. This local computability is precisely what distinguishes predictive coding from standard backpropagation in terms of biological plausibility: backpropagation requires that backward-pass error signals be carried by the exact transpose of the forward-pass weight matrix (the weight transport problem) and that a single global scalar loss be defined at a designated output layer–neither of which has a known biological implementation 48. Predictive coding sidesteps both constraints because each node carries its own loss and gradient computation requires only message-passing between directly connected populations.

Therefore, a particularly unifying formal move is to treat the brain’s generative model as a factor graph (or equivalent graphical representation) and view cortical computation as message passing that updates local sufficient statistics (beliefs) until global consistency constraints are satisfied. In this view, predictive coding corresponds to one important regime of variational message passing (especially under Gaussian/Laplace assumptions), while belief propagation / Bethe-style approximations become relevant for more discrete or structured latent variables (one discrete belief propagation formulation, Bio-RCN, is covered in the "Laminar Error Signals" subsection of "Cortical Error Signals") 45, 50. This reframes "prediction units" and "error units" as an algorithmic partition of messages rather than as a commitment to a particular anatomical ladder. The deepest invariance across these formalisms is not "hierarchy," but local computability. Regardless of whether the global dependency structure is a chain, a tree, or a loopy graph, the cortical algorithm remains: (i) maintain local beliefs about latent causes; (ii) receive local "context" messages from connected populations; (iii) compute local mismatches; (iv) update activity quickly and weights slowly to reduce a shared variational objective. This is why predictive frameworks remain plausible in a cortex whose wiring departs strongly from a feedforward stack. A predictive-coding graph model allows different connectivity patterns (Figure). The model implements predictive coding on a general graph (Figure).

The resulting intuition that each neuron/column has its own "cognitive light cone" 51 can be made precise with Markov blankets: for any subsystem (a neuron, microcircuit, column, area, or network), a Markov blanket is a statistical boundary–sensory and active states–that renders internal states conditionally independent of external states given the blanket. In cortical terms, a neuron’s (or column’s) effective world is the set of variables that can influence it through its blanket; everything outside is "seen" only indirectly, via messages mediated by intermediate blankets. Importantly, a unit’s blanket-defined lightcone is not restricted to other cortical populations: it can encompass thalamic relay and modulatory inputs, basal-ganglia and cerebellar return projections, hippocampal signals, interoceptive and proprioceptive afferents, and diffuse neuromodulatory tone. "Prediction error" at a cortical node can therefore reflect mismatches with motor efference copies, expected reward-prediction errors, visceral states, or mnemonic reactivations–not only sensory reconstruction 2, 3. This dissolves the apparent boundary between perception and action: a motor-cortical neuron predicting proprioceptive reafference, a prefrontal neuron predicting the temporal pattern of dopaminergic reward-prediction errors, and a V1 neuron predicting retinal input are all performing the same operation–local free-energy minimization–over different cognitive lightcones.

Markov blankets can be nested across scales (neurons ⊂\subset columns ⊂\subset areas ⊂\subset networks), providing a principled way to talk about multiscale modularity without assuming a single global hierarchy 52. A similar perspective is that the cortex contains many semi-autonomous predictive models operating in parallel (often anchored in different reference frames, modalities, or sensorimotor contingencies) that must be coordinated by long-range connections. On this view, cortex is not merely hierarchical but heterarchical: different subnetworks can be "higher" or "lower" depending on the variable being predicted, the timescale in play, and the current task demands 53. Even within a single cortical area, lateral connections enable neighboring columns to predict each other’s activity–supporting intra-areal contextual phenomena such as surround suppression and contour integration 54–so that "levels" of prediction exist not only across areas but also within them. This raises the question: if hierarchy is not a strict ladder, what are cortical "levels"? A robust operational definition is: a "level" corresponds to a set of latent variables sharing (i) a characteristic timescale (temporal receptive window / intrinsic timescale), (ii) a characteristic granularity (fine sensory causes vs coarse abstract causes), and (iii) a characteristic conditional dependency neighborhood (who sends/receives messages to whom). Under this definition, cortex supports multiple overlapping hierarchies (sensory, motor, interoceptive/visceromotor, social-cognitive, etc.) that interlock via shared factors and rich-club hubs, rather than a single canonical chain.

In summary, the cortical predictive-coding framework does not require–and the anatomy does not support–a single chain-like hierarchy. The global free energy decomposes into a sum of local losses over nodes in a directed graph that may include lateral, skip, and recurrent edges; each node minimizes precision-weighted prediction error using only locally available signals, sidestepping the weight-transport and global-loss constraints that make backpropagation biologically implausible. The "cognitive lightcone" of any cortical unit–formalized via nested Markov blankets–extends beyond other cortical areas to encompass thalamic, subcortical, interoceptive, proprioceptive, and neuromodulatory afferents, so that prediction error can reflect mismatches with any structured regularity in a unit’s input, not only sensory reconstruction. "Levels" of the hierarchy are therefore best defined operationally–by shared timescale, representational granularity, and conditional-dependency neighborhood–yielding multiple overlapping hierarchies (sensory, motor, interoceptive, social-cognitive) interlocked via shared factors and rich-club hubs, rather than a single canonical ladder.

Constraints and regularizers

The above loss functions do not operate in a vacuum. Cortical learning unfolds within a biological substrate that imposes additional costs and hard constraints–some of which can be interpreted as implicit regularizers on the optimization, others as inviolable boundary conditions. Together, these shape the effective loss landscape in ways that go well beyond "minimize prediction error." We enumerate them here; the mechanisms by which cortex accommodates each are deferred to forthcoming sections (especially the "Cortical Plasticity" and "Plasticity" sections).

The complexity cost is itself a regularizer. The KL-divergence term in Eq. 1–DKL[qϕ(z|x)||pθ(z)]D_{KL}[q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z)]–already penalizes posteriors that deviate excessively from the prior, functioning as an intrinsic Occam’s razor that favors parsimonious explanations of sensory data 1, 2. This is not a separate constraint bolted onto the loss but a structural feature of variational inference: minimizing free energy inherently trades off accuracy against complexity. Nevertheless, the strength of this regularization is set by the precision of the prior, which is itself learned and modulated–meaning the effective weight of the complexity penalty is adaptive rather than fixed.

Metabolic cost. The brain consumes roughly 20% of the body’s resting metabolic budget despite comprising  2% of body mass, and cortical spiking, synaptic transmission, and dendritic integration account for the bulk of this expenditure 55. This relentless metabolic pressure acts as an implicit L1/L0L_1/L_0-like penalty on neural activity and synaptic maintenance, favoring: The study tests stability of its trained networks (Figure) 91. A 2025 spiking-network study includes an energy-related training objective (Figure).

Sparse, efficient coding. Representations in which only a small fraction of neurons are active at any time minimize metabolic cost per bit of transmitted information 56, 57. Sparsity also decorrelates population activity, reducing redundancy across units–linking metabolic pressure to classical efficient-coding and redundancy-reduction objectives 58, 59. A recurrent-network model tests energy-efficient prediction (Figure) 87. The model measures energy-related cost and prediction (Figure).

Wiring-length minimization. Axonal and dendritic arbors are metabolically expensive to build and maintain. The observed compactness of cortical wiring–local clustering, topographic maps, the small-world architecture described above–can be understood as an optimization that minimizes total wiring cost subject to computational connectivity requirements 60, 61.

Stability constraints. A system that updates billions of synapses in real time to reduce prediction error faces a constant threat of destabilization. Several interacting constraints enforce stability: A model couples excitatory and inhibitory plasticity (Figure) 88. The model tests how local synaptic interactions affect stability (Figure).

Homeostatic regulation of firing rates. Cortical neurons must maintain their mean firing rates and population activity levels within a viable dynamic range; unchecked Hebbian potentiation would drive runaway excitation, while unchecked depression would silence circuits entirely 62, 63. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms (synaptic scaling, intrinsic excitability adjustment, metaplasticity) function as implicit constraints that bound the operating point of the network.

Excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance. Cortical networks operate in a regime of approximate balance between excitation and inhibition, which is critical for maintaining sensitivity to inputs, preventing epileptiform runaway, and supporting the irregular, asynchronous firing regime observed in vivo 64, 65. Perturbations to E/I balance must be corrected on timescales faster than or commensurate with learning-driven weight changes–imposing a constraint that shapes which synaptic updates are permissible at any moment.

Synaptic normalization. Total synaptic strength onto a neuron cannot grow without bound; multiplicative or subtractive normalization of synaptic weights acts as an implicit constraint analogous to weight decay or norm penalties in machine learning 66, 67.

Consolidation and catastrophic-interference avoidance. New learning must not overwrite previously consolidated representations that remain useful. This stability-plasticity tradeoff 68 imposes what amounts to a regularization toward previously learned weight configurations–implemented through mechanisms such as metaplasticity, synaptic tagging and capture, and sleep-dependent consolidation, discussed in later sections. The study compares continual-learning algorithms (Figure) 90. A continual-learning study models the balance between learning and retention (Figure).

Dale’s law. Each cortical neuron releases a single principal neurotransmitter (or co-transmitter complement) at all of its axonal terminals–excitatory neurons remain excitatory and inhibitory neurons remain inhibitory across all their postsynaptic targets 69, 70. This is a hard constraint, not a soft penalty: it partitions the weight matrix into sign-constrained submatrices and fundamentally shapes what credit-assignment solutions are reachable, distinguishing cortical learning from unconstrained artificial networks in which any weight can take any sign 71.

Biophysical stochasticity. Synaptic transmission is probabilistically unreliable (vesicle release probability at central synapses is often well below 1), ion-channel gating is stochastic, and spike generation is noisy–particularly in the low-firing-rate regime characteristic of cortex in vivo 70, 72. This irreducible stochasticity means that every gradient signal the cortex computes is corrupted by noise, effectively imposing a floor on the precision of any single synaptic update and favoring learning rules that are robust to high-variance gradient estimates–an implicit regularization analogous to the beneficial effects of stochastic gradient noise in machine learning 73.

Capacity constraints. The cortex, despite its vast scale, has a finite number of neurons, synapses, and dendritic compartments, and individual synaptic weights are stored with limited precision–estimated at roughly 4-5 bits per synapse based on spine-volume measurements 74. These finite-capacity and finite-precision constraints force the system to compress high-dimensional sensory streams into lower-dimensional latent representations, favoring the extraction of abstract, generalizable statistical regularities over rote memorization of individual experiences.

These constraints and costs do not merely limit cortical learning–they shape it, pushing the system toward sparse, balanced, stable, and metabolically efficient solutions that generalize well. How, precisely, cortex satisfies these constraints through specific plasticity mechanisms is the subject of the sections that follow.

Relationship with superordinate objectives

The cortical loss functions developed above–variational free energy and its temporal, active, and regularized extensions–specify the computational form of cortical optimization. But the content of that optimization–which prior preferences are installed, what counts as a "good" model, and what experiences are actively sought–is set by the superordinate objectives: intrinsic motivation, empowerment, and social control. Each maps onto a distinct aspect of the cortical loss landscape.

Intrinsic motivation enters through both components of the free-energy objective. The complexity term DKL[q(z|x)∥p(z)]D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q(z|x)\|p(z)] is explicitly a coding cost–minimizing it implements the compression drive toward maximally compact, high-fidelity world models 75, 1. The metabolic and sparsity constraints tighten this compression further, penalizing the energy cost per bit of representation. The learning progress component–the drive to seek experiences that most rapidly improve the model–maps onto the epistemic value term in expected free energy: the expected reduction in posterior entropy 𝔼q(oτ|π)[DKL[q(sτ|oτ,π)∥q(sτ|π)]]\mathbb{E}_{q(o_\tau|\pi)}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}[q(s_\tau|o_\tau,\pi)\|q(s_\tau|\pi)]], which quantifies how much a predicted observation would tighten beliefs about hidden causes 42, 76. Policies maximizing epistemic value steer the organism toward state-space regions where its model is poorest and learning fastest–formally connecting Schmidhuber’s compression progress to the epistemic component of EFE 77. The temporal hierarchy ensures this curiosity drive is itself hierarchically structured, with fast-timescale exploration nested within slower epistemic campaigns at higher cortical levels. An active-inference model explores an uncertain T-maze (Figure) 89. The model replans as information arrives (Figure).

Empowerment is supported by the sensorimotor structure of the cortical generative model. The action-conditioned state-transition function fθ(zt,at)f_\theta(z_t, a_t)–present, per the APC framework, at every cortical level 4–provides the forward model required to compute and maximize the channel capacity between actions and future states 78, 79. Within the EFE framework, empowerment emerges as a natural prior preference when the agent’s objective includes maintaining influence over its future: if prior preferences favor maximally diverse reachable states, policy selection approximates empowerment maximization 78. The two APC error streams–state-transition prediction errors (refining the forward model) and action-prediction errors (refining the policy)–jointly optimize the agent’s model of its own controllability.

Social control enters through prior preferences p(oτ)p(o_\tau) over social outcomes–being recognized, maintaining status, preserving relational bonds–whose violation generates high pragmatic prediction error within the EFE 80, 81. The cortical timescale hierarchy is directly relevant: the slowest dynamics in transmodal apex cortex (medial prefrontal, default-mode regions) encode the most temporally extended latent causes, including self-referential and mentalizing representations 22, 25. In the loss framework, these apex regions maintain slowly evolving priors about identity and social role–deep generative priors updated only by strong, sustained prediction error, lending the self-model its characteristic persistence. Social context further reshapes the effective loss via precision-weighting: social attention and social threat modulate the gain on prediction errors related to others’ evaluations and intentions, making them disproportionately influential on inference and learning 10. At the highest levels, the generative model extends to include other agents’ beliefs and generative models, so that inter-agent prediction-error minimization–reducing divergence between one’s own model and the inferred models of significant others–becomes a formal expression of the drive toward mutual understanding 81, 80.

In sum, variational free energy provides the mathematical form of the cortical loss; the three superordinate objectives determine its functional content. Intrinsic motivation is realized through the complexity term and the epistemic EFE component. Empowerment is realized through the action-conditioned generative model and the pragmatic EFE component (achieving controllable outcomes). Social control is realized through prior preferences over social observations, the slow self-model at the cortical apex, and the embedding of other minds within the generative hierarchy. The biological constraints–metabolic cost, sparsity, stability, Dale’s law, finite capacity–shape all three equally, delimiting which solutions cortex can reach. In this sense, each precision-weighted prediction error, at each level and timescale, is a local signal that–aggregated across the full spatiotemporal hierarchy–moves the system toward greater compression, greater controllability, and greater social coherence.
